subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: The big word for the unit is data. It sounds hard, but it is simple: data is information — numbers, words, pictures or sounds. When Leila counts the mangoes in the bowl, that is data. When Leo sorts his blocks into a red pile and a blue pile, he is being a data detective. A computing device is a machine that works with data, and it can answer our questions (a phone tells us the weather, a watch counts our steps).
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games
Apply, explain and finish the Unit Project and Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 1 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: Say that data is information — numbers, words, pictures or sounds.
Say that a computing device works with data and can answer questions, and name one (a phone, a tablet, a watch).
Sort real things into groups that are the same in some way (by colour, size or kind).
Count how many things are in each group.
Colour a tiny block graph to show how many — one block for each thing.
Organise things by putting them in order (small to big, or 1, 2, 3).
These are spoken, hands-on skills — the child does not need to read or write to show them. Pointing, sorting and colouring are enough.

concepts.title: Data is all around us
concepts.explanation: Data is a fancy word for information. Data can be numbers, words, pictures or sounds. A computing device — like a phone, a tablet or a watch — is a machine that works with data. The best part: a computing device can answer our questions. This is a computing device. It is full of data — pictures, sounds, numbers. And it can answer our questions! Watch. What is the weather today?
concepts.example: See — it gave us an answer. That answer is data too.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you name one computing device?

concepts.title: Sorting into groups
concepts.explanation: To sort means to put things into groups. Things in the same group are the same in some way. We can sort by colour (all the red ones together), by size (all the big ones together), or by kind (all the animals together, all the fruit together). Tip out your basket of objects in the middle of the circle. Oh dear, all mixed up! Let us sort them — all the same-colour ones together. This is a group. Every one is red.
concepts.example: We sorted by colour. Look, we can sort the same things in more than one way!
concepts.checkYourself: you are all red. you are all big. Can you make a group where everything is the same in some way?

concepts.title: Count each group and make a block graph
concepts.explanation: Once we have sorted things into groups, we can count each group to see how many. When we colour one block for each thing, we make a little picture of our data. This picture is called a block graph. A block graph makes it very easy to see which group has the most and which has the fewest. Go back to your sorted groups from Session 2. 1, 2, 3, 4 — four red ones. Now show you the magic. Let us make a picture of this. For every red one, I colour one block. Watch. Now we can SEE it.
concepts.example: Which row is longer? That group has the most!
concepts.checkYourself: Can you colour the right number of blocks? Can you point to the row with the most? Can you count a small group correctly (touching each one)?

concepts.title: Putting things in order
concepts.explanation: To organise data means to put it in order. We can put things in order by size — from the smallest to the biggest. We can put numbers in order — 1, 2, 3, 4. When data is in a good order, it is much easier to read. Muddle them up and ask: “Who is tallest? It is hard to tell.” Now line them up shortest to tallest: “Now it is easy!
concepts.example: We put them in order by size.” Do the same with three objects — a small stone, a bigger one, the biggest. Choose three you of different heights (kindly, only if they are happy to help).
concepts.checkYourself: Can you tell which is shortest and which is longest? Can you understand that order helps us read data? Can you put three things in order by size?

concepts.title: Be a data detective! (class survey)
concepts.explanation: A data detective asks a question, collects the answers (the data), sorts and counts each group, shows you on a block graph, and reads the graph to find the answer. This session runs the Mini-Project, “Our Favourite Fruit”. Detectives, here is our question: which fruit does our class like best — mango, banana or apple? Let us find out with data! We are collecting our data.
concepts.example: Do it yourself: be a data detective! (class survey). Work through it slowly, then check what you did against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you help count a group and colour the graph? Can you point to the favourite (the most) on the finished graph? Can you take part in collecting the data?

activities.title: Our Favourite Fruit
activities.materials: A sheet of paper and a pencil — no computer needed for this one
steps: Our question: Which fruit does our class like best — mango, banana or apple?
Ask each friend: mango, banana or apple?
Make one mark for each answer. That is our data!
Count how many chose each fruit.
Colour one block for you on the graph below.
Look at the graph. Which fruit has the most blocks? That is our class favourite!

activities.title: Our Favourite Fruit: This is your real class data, so there is no single right answer. Check that each child was counted once, that the graph has one block per child with no gaps, and that the child can point to the fruit with the most blocks (the class favourite) and the one with the fewest. Worked example: if mango = 5, banana = 3, apple = 2, then the favourite is mango, the fewest is apple, and 10 children answered in all.
activities.materials: A sheet of paper and a pencil — no computer needed for this one
steps: Practice (the printed graph shows mango = 4, banana = 2, apple = 3)
How many liked mango? 4.
Mango (the longest row, 4 blocks). Which fruit did the most you like?
Banana (the shortest row, 2 blocks). Which fruit did the fewest you like?
How many liked apple? 3.
Numbers in order, smallest first: 1, 2, 3.

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

steps: Plan first: write down what your be a data detective project has to do before you build anything.
Build the smallest version that does one of those things, and run it.
Add one feature at a time, testing after each one.
When something breaks, change one thing, run it again, and note what fixed it.
Check your work against every success criterion below before you call it finished.
successCriteria: I asked my friends the question.
I made one mark for each answer.
I coloured one block for each child, with no gaps.
I found our class favourite fruit (the most).
2. Which fruit did the MOST children like? ______________________

selfAssessment: I can say that data is information — numbers, words, pictures or sounds.
I can say that a computing device works with data and can answer questions, and name one (a phone, a tablet, a watch).
I can sort real things into groups that are the same in some way (by colour, size or kind).
I can count how many things are in each group.
I can colour a tiny block graph to show how many — one block for each thing.
I can organise things by putting them in order (small to big, or 1, 2, 3).
I can these are spoken, hands-on skills — the child does not need to read or write to show them. Pointing, sorting and colouring are enough.
